Autograd normally saves intermediate activations needed by backward. Checkpointing saves only selected boundaries and reruns the intervening forward computations during backward. Parameters and optimizer state are unchanged; the saving is chiefly activation memory. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.06174)

If an ordinary step costs one forward $F$ plus backward approximately $2F$, recomputing one forward changes $3F$ to $4F$, about 33% extra arithmetic. This is a rough model, not a guaranteed runtime penalty. Selective checkpointing, fused attention, communication overlap, and kernel costs alter it.

For a chain of $L$ similarly sized layers, checkpointed segments can reduce stored boundary/interior activations toward $O(\sqrt L)$ under a suitable schedule. Preserve RNG behavior for dropout and handle mutable state carefully; rerunning a stateful forward can otherwise change the function being differentiated. [4](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/index.html)
